Notoriety is the state of being widely known — but specifically for something bad, wrong, shameful, or scandalous.

Think of it as fame's darker twin. It means people know who you are, people talk about you, people remember your name — but not because you did something admirable. Because you did something notorious.
The Single Most Important Thing to Understand

This word carries a built-in negative judgment. It is not a neutral word.

If someone says "She achieved great fame," that sounds like a compliment.
If someone says "She achieved great notoriety," that is not a compliment — it means she became well-known for something bad or disgraceful.

This is the heart of the word. Never forget it.
What Kinds of Things Earn Someone Notoriety?

• A criminal who commits a shocking crime
  • A politician caught in a massive corruption scandal
  • A company that poisoned a river and got exposed on the news
  • A person who lied publicly and was found out by millions

These people and things become known — but for all the wrong reasons. That wide, unwanted, negative recognition is their notoriety.

These three words are easy to confuse, so it helps to understand them side by side.

Fame is simply being widely known. It is neutral to positive. A talented musician, a great scientist, a beloved actor — they have fame.

Notoriety is being widely known for something negative or disreputable. The negativity is the key ingredient. A fraudster, a cheater, a corrupt official — they have notoriety.

Infamy is very similar to notoriety but tends to be used for extreme or historic wrongdoing — the kind of evil or disgrace that is remembered across generations. Think of war criminals, tyrants, or catastrophic events. Infamy is essentially the deepest, most severe form of negative fame. Notoriety can apply to smaller-scale scandals and wrongdoing too. So: all infamy involves notoriety, but not all notoriety rises to infamy.
The Adjective That Helps You Lock In the Meaning

The adjective form is notorious, and it may actually be more familiar to you. If you've ever heard someone call a person or place "notorious," it means they are widely known for something bad. A notorious liar. A notorious crime boss. A notorious scam.

Notoriety is simply the noun that names that condition. A notorious person has notoriety. This connection can make the noun easier to remember.

• The gang leader's notoriety spread across the entire city after the bank robbery.

(Everyone knew who he was — but because of his crimes.)

  • The restaurant gained notoriety after a health inspector found serious violations in the kitchen.

(It became "famous" — but for a bad reason.)

  • She had spent years trying to rebuild her career after the notoriety from the scandal.

(Her bad reputation had followed her.)

  • The dictator's notoriety was so great that historians still study his crimes today.

(He is widely remembered — but for horrible reasons.)
A Common Modern Misuse — and Why It Matters

In casual, everyday speech, some people use notoriety to simply mean "fame" or "recognition," without any negative meaning attached — as if it were just a fancy synonym for being well-known.

This is considered incorrect in careful, precise usage. If you write "The young scientist gained notoriety for her groundbreaking discovery," a careful reader will raise an eyebrow, because the word implies her discovery was somehow shameful or wrong — which you probably didn't mean.

For positive or neutral recognition, use fame, recognition, renown, or prominence instead. Reserve notoriety strictly for cases where the reason for being well-known is bad, negative, or at least controversial.

Here is a simple way to feel the word from the inside:

Imagine doing something embarrassing or wrong, and then the whole world finds out. Everyone is talking about it. Your name is everywhere — but for a reason that makes you cringe or feel ashamed. That spread of negative recognition, that unwanted dark fame — that is your notoriety.
Notoriety is the state of being widely known and talked about — but for something bad, wrong, or disgraceful, not for something admirable.
